title: Stochastic eviction schedulers for paged KV cache
body:
Summary:
This note collects design ideas and early experiment results for a low-overhead, robust eviction scheduler for the paged KV cache used by our serving runtime. Goal: keep tail latency low under mixed workloads (many short context chat vs long inference), avoid pathological eviction storms caused by pure LRU on adversarial or bursty access patterns, and enable fusion-friendly data layouts for downstream kernel optimizations (e.g., combined gather + softmax for FlashAttention variants).

Motivation / problem statement:
- Paged KV cache: we partition KV memory into pages (page == contiguous chunk of KV entries for a set of tokens across layers) to allow on-demand resident sets and to spill cold pages without per-token fragmentation.
- Simple LRU or strict LFU leads to brittle behavior when workload has: repeated short chats interleaved with large generation requests, periodic replay of prompts, or many requests with overlapping prefixes.
- Eviction is an implicit control knob for latency: evicting a hot page right before a burst causes a remote fetch or re-populate that increases p95/p99. Conversely, holding too many pages reduces capacity for large requests and increases throughput variability.

Design concept: stochastic multi-queue scheduler with asynchronous scavenger
We propose a hybrid scheduler combining:
1) multi-queue aging buckets (tiny fixed number of queues, e.g., 8) approximating recency+frequency;
2) stochastic eviction probability shaping per-bucket (adds randomized chance to evict older-but-frequently-used pages to avoid pathological anchors);
3) background asynchronous scavenger threads that perform non-blocking prefetch/eviction decisions off the critical serving path;
4) burst detection window to temporarily raise retention thresholds for pages matching recent request prefixes.

Why stochastic?
- Randomized eviction reduces worst-case sequences that intentionally or accidentally cause thrashing.
- It smooths out eviction waves: instead of evicting a whole contiguous set deterministically, we probabilistically drop subset which lets the cache partially adapt without mass misses.

Scheduler pseudocode (high-level):
- On page access: bump bucket = (bucket + 1) & mask; increment access counter, update last_seen_ts
- Periodic (every 2–8 ms) background tick: for each page in lowest-residency buckets evaluate p_evict = base_rate * decay_factor(bucket_age) * (1 - burst_boost(page_prefix)) + randomness(); if rand() < p_evict && residency > min_resident -> mark_for_eviction_async
- Async evict worker: coalesce adjacent page evictions, writeback/spill if dirty, free memory and publish capacity event
- Prefetch heuristic: when request pattern shows repeated misses for same page within short window (prefix match >= 0.6), schedule prefetch with small priority token (best-effort) that can be cancelled if burst subsides

Integration with kernel fusion and FlashAttention variants:
- Motivation: each remote/populate of a page has cost; we want kernel paths that (a) reduce number of kernel launches while (b) avoid heavy divergences that kill occupancy.
- Proposal: expose a compact page residency bitmap per-request that kernels can consume to implement "gather-if-resident" paths. For example, a fused gather+masked-softmax kernel that takes the residency bitmap and performs: gather resident KV from local buffer, compute attention for resident items, and optionally emit fallbacks for missing entries (either zeroed or trigger a lightweight hold-and-retry).
- This lets us reduce host-device synchronizations: kernel can iterate resident-only tokens in-register, while missing tokens are accounted for by a small masked reduce step.

Microbench experiment plan (done so far):
- Setup: 8x A100, runtime candidate implementing basic stochastic scheduler with 8 queues, 2 async scavenger threads. Workloads: (A) many short chat messages (mean length 20 tokens, arrival 50 qps), (B) mixed long generations (mean length 1024 tokens, arrival 2 qps), (C) synthetic adversarial sequence flipping hot pages every 5 requests.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency for token generation, percent of requests hitting resident-only path, kernel occupancy, eviction churn (pages evicted per minute).
- Results (abbreviated):
  * Workload A: resident-hit rose from 72% -> 80% vs baseline LRU; p99 improved 18ms -> 14ms (20% improvement). Eviction churn down 12%.
  * Workload B: little change in resident-hit (baseline 62% -> 63%); slight p50 improvement (3%).
  * Workload C (adversarial): baseline LRU collapsed with eviction storm (resident-hit 28% p99 spike); stochastic scheduler maintained 46% resident-hit and bounded p99 significantly (reduction from 220ms -> 95ms in token tail).
- Notes: these are early runs with 512KB page sizes. Smaller page sizes increase bookkeeping overhead; larger sizes increase wasted memory on partial hotness.

Implementation notes / data structures:
- Page metadata struct (kept in L1 cache-friendly array): page_id, bucket_idx, last_seen_ts (int64), access_counter (uint32), prefix_hash (uint32), resident_flag (bool), dirty_flag (bool), approx_size (uint32). Keep struct <= 32 bytes to aid scan performance during ticks.
- Buckets are simple singly-linked lists of page indices stored in a pre-allocated vector; bucket rotations use atomic pointers to avoid locks on hot path.
- Eviction marking is done with atomic CAS on resident_flag then queued to a lock-free ring for async scavengers.
- To reduce atomic contention we maintain per-warp or per-thread local counters and flush them to global every N operations.

Prefetch prioritization and cancellation:
- Prefetch entries carry a priority score based on recent hit-rate and predicted upcoming usage (very small ML model running in control plane or simple EWMA).
- Prefetches are cooperative: if an incoming request arrives and requires the page immediately, it can block-on-prefetch up to a short timeout (configurable, default 3ms) otherwise it falls back to partial-resident kernel.
- Cancellation: prefetch tasks include a cheap cancellation flag polled by worker; if cancellation occurs before device memcpy starts, we drop the task to save bandwidth.

Fusion considerations (kernel-level):
- Aim: minimize global memory roundtrips and kernel launches. We experimented with two strategies:
  1) "Resident-first fused kernel": single kernel that loads resident pages values via direct device pointers and computes attention contributions, writing scratch partials back to a per-request buffer. Missing tokens are counted and returned to host for follow-up.
  2) "Fallback ping-pong": small fused kernel that computes attention over resident tokens and at the end posts a compact list of missing ranges to host which then issues a blocking populate and a short follow-up kernel for the missing region.
- We found strategy (1) produced better tail-latency for mixed workloads because it avoids a second kernel launch in common case. Strategy (2) has simpler control flow and slightly better throughput for reads-only massive batches where miss rate is near zero.

Observed tradeoffs:
- Randomized eviction reduces worst-case but introduces non-determinism in performance; harder to reproduce exactly in postmortems. We must capture rich telemetry (eviction decisions, bucket states) to correlate.
- Async scavenger threads reduce critical-path stalls but need careful coalescing to avoid PCIe/host saturation when many pages are spilled/populated concurrently. We added a simple token-bucket at the async worker to cap copy throughput.
- Prefetch aggressiveness is workload-sensitive: too aggressive saturates bandwidth and nudges out pages needed shortly after. We rely on short lived EWMA to adapt pref threshold.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Optimum page size for different model families (LLaMA-like vs. dense transformer variants) — run systematic grid over page size {64KB, 128KB, 256KB, 512KB}.
- Better prefix similarity metric: present approach uses 32-bit hash of last K tokens; consider locality-sensitive hashing or reservoir-sampled fingerprints.
- Kernel-level API for "resident bitmap" consumption: define a compact ABI for fused kernels to read page-residency metadata without host roundtrip. Prototype candidate: 64-bit residency words per request, passed as device pointer in kernel launch params.
- Quantify memory overhead of metadata vs resident capacity (target <= 1.5% overhead).

Operational notes / instrumentation:
- Emit structured traces when: eviction storms occur (eviction rate > X/min), prefetch cancellations exceed 10% in a minute, async worker queue depth > 256.
- Collect histograms of per-page inter-arrival times; generate alerts when distribution becomes multi-modal (indicator of mixed workload causing thrash).

Next steps:
- Short-term (2 weeks): stabilize scheduler code path, add telemetry hooks, run page-size sweep on bench infra, and produce a turnkey config for Dedicated clusters.
- Medium-term (1–3 months): implement fused resident-gather-softmax prototype and measure p50/p99 on production traces; add a simple ML-based prefetch scorer in control plane that uses request features.

Appendix: lightweight scheduler pseudocode
for each request r:
  pages = find_pages(r.prefix)
  for p in pages:
    bucket = p.bucket_idx
    atomic_inc(p.local_hits)
    if p.resident: use_local(p)
    else: record_miss(p)

background_tick():
  for bucket in buckets_low_to_high:
    for p in sample(bucket, sample_k):
      age = now - p.last_seen_ts
      base = base_eviction_rate(bucket)
      burst = burst_boost_for_prefix(p.prefix_hash)
      p_evict = clamp(base * decay(age) * (1 - burst) + uniform_random(0, rscale), 0, 1)
      if rand() < p_evict and p.resident and p.residency > min:
        if CAS(p.resident, true, false): enqueue_async_eviction(p)

async_eviction_worker():
  while pop(evict_queue, p):
    coalesce_adjacent_pages(p)
    if p.dirty: writeback(p)
    free_device_memory(p)
    publish_capacity_event(p)

References / related tickets:
- PROJ-8921: paged-KV cache redesign spec (linked above)
- PR #4312: initial stochastic-scheduler prototype (see linked_artifacts)
- Slack discussion: #serving-runtime thread on stochastic vs deterministic eviction (2024-11-20)

Notes to reviewers: prioritize verifying scalability under bursty admission patterns and check that telemetry is sufficient to reproduce eviction storms. Suggest pairing with SRE to run chaos tests that reorder requests and simulate delayed prefetches.

-- Ava
